unesco.title: Huaconada, ritual dance of Mito
unesco.description: Huaconada is a ritual dance performed in the village of Mito in the province of Concepción in the central Peruvian Andes. Every year, on the first three days of January, masked men known as ''huacones'' perform a choreographed series of dances in the centre of the town. The ''huacones'' represent the former council of elders, and for the duration of Huaconada they become the town’s highest authority. The ''tronador'' (whip) they carry and their masks emphasize this role, the latter characterized by accentuated noses that evoke the beak of the condor, creature that represents the spirit of the sacred mountains. The dance involves two types of ''huacones:'' elders who wear traditional costumes and finely-carved masks inspiring respect and fear; and modern ''huacones'' who wear colourful dress, their masks embodying terror, sadness or mockery. During Huaconada, the modern ''huacones'' dance circumscribed steps around the elders, who have greater freedom to dance improvised movements because of their seniority. An orchestra plays different rhythms, beating out time on a small indigenous drum called a ''tinya.'' Huaconada synthesizes distinctive elements from the Andes and Spain while incorporating new, modern elements. Only those of good conduct and moral integrity may become ''huacones.'' The dance is traditionally passed on from father to son, while clothing and masks are also inherited.

profile.name: Huaconada
profile.tagline: Ritual masked dance of Mito, Peru, performed by elders as village authority in January.
profile.insight: For three days each January, masked huacones embody the village’s highest authority, wielding whips and condor-beaked masks to dance respect and fear into the streets of Mito.
profile.profile: Huaconada is a ritual dance from Mito, Peru, performed annually on January 1–3 by masked men called huacones who represent the former council of elders. Two types of huacones appear: elders in traditional costumes with fearsome carved masks, and younger dancers in colorful modern dress with expressive masks. The dance is accompanied by the tinya, a small indigenous drum, and features choreographed and improvised movements reflecting moral authority. The tradition is inherited father to son, restricted to men of good conduct.
profile.profile_long:
The Huaconada is a ritual dance performed in the village of Mito, located in the province of Concepción in the central Peruvian Andes. Every year, on the first three days of January, the village undergoes a transformation as a group of men known as 'huacones' assume the role of the town’s highest authority, symbolizing the ancient council of elders. This tradition, inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2010, synthesizes elements from the Andes and Spain while incorporating contemporary influences. The dance is strictly inherited from father to son, and participation is reserved for men of good conduct and moral integrity, as the huacones are expected to uphold the village's social order.

The visual identity of the dance centers on the mask, which features a prominent nose resembling the beak of a condor, a creature representing the spirit of the sacred mountains. There are two distinct classes of huacones. The elders wear traditional costumes and finely carved, coarse masks that inspire respect and fear. In contrast, younger huacones wear colorful modern dress and masks that express terror, sadness, or mockery. The costume includes a wool hat or artisanal 'chuco', a serge blanket used as a cape, a black pant with a white apron, wool socks, and 'llanque' sandals made of ox hide. Each performer carries a 'tronador', a whip made of ox hide with a wooden handle, which serves as a symbol of their authority.

The choreography is structured around the interaction between these two groups. Younger huacones perform circumscribed steps around the elders, who possess the seniority to dance with greater freedom and are permitted to improvise their movements. Specific figures, such as 'cuti cuti' (involving circular movements), 'Inti Palpoy', and 'Anca Palpoy', are linked to the ritual customs of the Andean people. The entire performance is guided by the rhythm of the 'tinya', a small indigenous drum, which dictates the tempo and structure of the dance. The whip, or 'tronador', is also used to represent the 'thunder crossing', reinforcing the huacones' authority over the village during their three-day tenure. As a sacred and restricted tradition, the Huaconada serves as a living connection between the past and present, maintaining the moral and social fabric of Mito through a performance that balances tradition, modernity, and the concept of the forbidden.

sections.origins_and_history: The Huaconada is a ritual dance of pre-Hispanic origin from the village of Mito. It represents a fusion of Andean and Spanish elements, serving as a moral and social guide for the community. In 2010, it was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed in the center of the village. Younger huacones perform circumscribed steps around the elders. Elders have the freedom to improvise their movements. The rhythm is set by the tinya drum. The whip, or tronador, is used as a symbol of authority.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is driven by an orchestra directed by the beat of the tinya, a small indigenous drum. The rhythm is described as a series of different rhythms played to accompany the choreographed and improvised movements.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear wool hats or 'chuco', serge blankets as capes, black pants, white aprons, wool socks, and 'llanque' sandals. Masks are made of wood with grotesque features and condor-beak noses. Whips made of ox hide with wooden handles are carried as symbols of authority.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance occurs annually on the first three days of January. The huacones represent the former council of elders and hold absolute power in the village during this period. It is a ritual of moral authority, respect, and fear.
sections.lineage: The tradition is passed from father to son, including the inheritance of clothing and masks.

profile.sacred_note: The dance is a restricted ritual performed only by men of good conduct and moral integrity; outsiders should observe with respect and not attempt to participate in the ritual authority roles.

teaching.formation: Center of the village; younger huacones circle the elders
teaching.level_notes: Restricted to men of good conduct; technique not described in sources

music_profile.sound_description: The music is defined by the steady, rhythmic beating of the tinya drum, which provides the tempo for the dancers' movements.

movement_profile.formation_and_space: Younger huacones dance in circles around the elders
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Do not attempt to perform as a huacone without being a member of the community and meeting the moral requirements.

episode_brief.logline: In the Andean village of Mito, a masked council of elders takes control for three days every January.
